name: New Zealand National Party
notes: Lead party of the 2023-2026 coalition government. Scored from its 2026 election policy pages and plan, the two 2023 coalition agreements it signed, and its governing record on the marker items. Coalition items demanded by ACT or NZ First are attributed to those parties in the rationale but count for National where it adopted them as government policy.

solidarity.rationale: National's 2026 programme is built on 'no new taxes', a return to surplus, debt below 40 per cent of GDP and core Crown spending falling towards 30 per cent of GDP, with 'spending restraint and ongoing fiscal discipline rather than introducing new taxes' and a stated aim of 'getting Kiwis off welfare and into work'. The coalition agreements it signed add benefit sanctions including electronic money management and stronger Jobseeker obligations. Against that it keeps the superannuation age at 65, extends paid parental leave to 30 weeks, makes KiwiSaver compulsory with a $1,500 payment at birth and retains the Winter Energy Payment, so this is self-reliance with a family-support floor rather than a minimal state.

regulation.rationale: Deregulation runs through the programme: engineers signing off building work without council inspection, an RMA replacement with 'more enabling rules', national standards to cut consenting costs, eliminating $1 billion of non-tariff barriers, and a Government Policy Statement on mining under the Fast-track Approvals Act. In government National passed ACT's Regulatory Standards Act, created a Ministry for Regulation, repealed Fair Pay Agreements, extended 90-day trials to all employers and narrowed the Reserve Bank to a single mandate. The exceptions are targeted interventions rather than a change of direction: a banking competition inquiry and stronger Grocery Commissioner powers (NZ First items), a rule that new data centres bring their own generation, and a government-backed Home Energy Fund for household loans.

liberty.rationale: 'Staying tough on crime' is one of National's four headline commitments: tougher sentences, a gang crackdown, 'more tools and powers for Police', abolishing good-character discounts for sexual offending and limiting sentencing discounts to 40 per cent. In government it restored Three Strikes, made gang membership an aggravating factor, funded more prison capacity and strengthened electronic monitoring, and passed the Electoral Amendment Act 2025 after the Attorney-General reported that ending same-day enrolment was inconsistent with the right to vote. The coalition agreements also carry liberty-positive items, ruling out hate speech legislation and requiring free-speech policies at funded tertiary providers, but those were NZ First and ACT demands rather than National's own programme.

tradition.rationale: National has no explicit social-values programme and treats conscience issues as personal votes; the coalition agreement leaves any End of Life Choice changes to a member's bill 'recognising this is a conscience issue'. Its 2026 material frames policy around 'strong families' and a 'property-owning democracy', and it agreed to NZ First's removal of the gender, sexuality and relationship education guidelines and to keeping women's sport free of 'rules relating to gender'. Its own consent-law reform points the other way. A mild traditional lean, with the caveat that the sharper items belong to a coalition partner.

institutions.rationale: National voted the Treaty Principles Bill down at its second reading on 10 April 2025 and refused a referendum on it, describing the bill as a crude way to handle a sensitive topic, and its coalition agreements commit to 'evidence-based' decisions with 'rigorous cost benefit analysis' and published public-service targets. Against that it legislated ministerial referral powers in the Fast-track Approvals Act, agreed to amend the Marine and Coastal Area Act in response to a Court of Appeal judgment and to 'refocus' the Waitangi Tribunal's scope, restored referendums on Māori wards, and passed the Electoral Amendment Act over a Bill of Rights inconsistency report. Process-minded in style but willing to override independent bodies when they obstruct its programme, so only a slight lean to institutions.

cosmopolitan.rationale: National is strongly outward-looking on trade, with new agreements, an India FTA and a target of doubling exports by 2034, and in government it liberalised skilled-migrant and seasonal-worker settings at ACT's request. But its coalition agreements commit to 'equal citizenship' over Treaty partnership: removing co-governance from public services, prioritising services 'on the basis of need, not race', declaring UNDRIP non-binding, a 'National Interest Test' before accepting UN agreements, and keeping the foreign-buyer ban. It voted down the Treaty Principles Bill and honours settlements. Economic openness combined with a citizens-first stance on identity and international obligations nets to a modest national lean.

environment.rationale: National keeps a net-zero-by-2050 commitment and doubling renewable electricity, and its 2026 Electrify NZ policy makes rooftop and on-farm solar permitted as of right with a Home Energy Fund for household loans. But the weight of the programme runs to growth: an RMA replacement with 'more enabling rules', a Government Policy Statement on mining under the Fast-track Approvals Act, and 'backing farmers to grow more'. In government it repealed the offshore oil and gas exploration ban, amended the Crown Minerals Act to promote extraction, stopped new Significant Natural Areas, agreed to review the methane target and cut cycleway spending. The Climate Change Commission's 2026 monitoring report found the second emissions budget at increasing risk and that recent government actions to reduce emissions are likely to be outweighed by actions that increase them.

diplomacy.rationale: The National-led government's Defence Capability Plan 2025 committed $12 billion over four years, $9 billion of it new, and a path to defence spending above 2 per cent of GDP within eight years, the highest since the early 1990s, for a 'combat-capable' force integrated more closely with Australia. National's 2026 Budget Responsibility Rules single out 'defence capability' as investment to continue. Its foreign policy emphasis otherwise runs through trade agreements and 'like-minded partners'. A clear strength lean, short of treating force as a primary instrument.

local.rationale: In 2023 National returned water assets to councils by scrapping Three Waters, promised city and regional deals, made medium-density housing rules optional for councils and considered sharing GST on new builds with them, all of which point local. Its 2026 programme points the other way: national standards for solar, quarries and gravel that apply 'as of right' over council rules, a single national Building Consent Authority for large projects, standardised zoning for small towns, and a fast-track regime in which ministers refer projects past local processes. Devolution of assets alongside centralisation of planning rules leaves a slight central lean.

change.rationale: National's 2026 pitch is continuity: 'by sticking to National's plan', 'fix the basics', reforms phased over years (paid parental leave up one week a year, KiwiSaver contributions rising to 12 per cent by 2032, surplus in 2028/29). Its first term was nonetheless sweeping in scale, with a 100-day plan of repeals, the RMA and NCEA replaced, the Māori Health Authority disestablished and a fast-track consenting regime, much of it reversing the previous government rather than building new systems. Cautious in framing and pace of new policy, expansive in undoing, which nets to a lean towards caution.
